strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in vision: improving generalization while balancing multiple tasks. Separately aggregating task-loss gradients and SAM corrections is a clear, modular idea compatible with MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, and IMTL.

Experiments span classification, 40-attribute prediction, and dense scene understanding, with consistent aggregate improvements over the corresponding base optimizers. For example, F-CAGrad improves MultiMNIST average accuracy from 95.01% to 95.95% and reduces CelebA average error from 8.52% to 8.22%. NYUv2 also shows improvements across several task metrics.

The sharpness trajectories, perturbation experiments, radius sweeps, and calibration measurements provide useful diagnostics beyond benchmark accuracy. Supplementary Tables 5–6 report consistently improved Brier scores and calibration errors.

Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 communicate the central mechanism effectively. The appendix supplies architectures and training schedules, and the underlying optimizers, datasets, and SAM/ASAM methods are appropriately attributed.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not isolated experimentally. There are no comparisons against SAM/ASAM applied to a scalarized multi-task loss or direct aggregation of per-task SAM gradients without the proposed decomposition. Shared-only and head-only perturbation ablations are also absent. Consequently, the results establish benefits from adding sharpness regularization, but do not establish the value of the distinctive aggregation rule.

The theoretical justification has substantive gaps. Theorems 1/4 describe a vector-valued maximum using a common shared perturbation, although different tasks need not admit a common maximizer; a componentwise interpretation only establishes separate task bounds. Algorithm 1 additionally perturbs shared and head parameters separately, whereas the bound jointly perturbs them. No analysis connects this blockwise approximation and the two separately aggregated gradient families to optimization of the stated bound. Appendix A also truncates Gaussian tails without stating the bounded-loss assumption needed for that step.

The implemented method is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.2 reports using adaptive SAM, while Equation 5 and Algorithm 1 describe ordinary Euclidean SAM. The corresponding adaptive perturbation and gradient decomposition are not provided. Selected perturbation radii and the validation-based selection procedure are also missing, and the asserted public implementation has no repository link in the manuscript.

The practical computational tradeoff is unquantified. Algorithm 1 requires task-specific perturbed evaluations and two gradient aggregations, yet no training-time, memory, or matched-compute comparison is reported. This matters particularly for the claimed applicability to 40-task CelebA.

The evidence supports aggregate improvements more strongly than coherent improvement of every task: on NYUv2, F-MGDA reduces segmentation mIoU from 30.47 to 26.42. The motivating low-resource and noisy-label settings are not directly evaluated. Furthermore, Tables 2–4 lack variability estimates, limiting interpretation of smaller gains. These concerns, together with the missing decisive controls and theoretical gaps, outweigh the promising benchmark results.
